{{orphan|date=September 2026}}
In [[linear algebra]], the '''quaternionic eigenvalue problem''' is the problem of determining the [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors#Matrices| eigenvalues and eigenvectors]] of a matrix with [[Quaternion#Definition|quaternionic]] entries. Unlike the [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors#Matrices|classical eigenvalue problem]]  over the complex numbers, where multiplication is [[Commutative property|commutative]], two distinct problems can be considered: the [[#Right eigenvalue problem|right eigenvalue problem]] and the [[#Left eigenvalue problem|left eigenvalue problem]].<ref name = HuangSo />{{rp|106}}

== History ==
The study of eigenvalues of quaternionic matrices began in the late 1940s with the work of H. C. Lee, who established quaternionic analogues of several classical results of matrix theory, including a version of  [[Schur's theorem|Shcur's triangularization theorem]].<ref name = Lee >{{Cite journal |last=Lee |first=H. C. |date=1948 |title=Eigenvalues and Canonical Forms of Matrices with Quaternion Coefficients |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy. Section A: Mathematical and Physical Sciences |volume=52 |pages=253–260 |jstor=20488503 }}</ref>{{rp|256}} Afterwards, N. A. Wiegmann established the existence of a [[Jordan normal form|Jordan canonical form]] for quaternionic matrices.<ref name = Wiegmann />{{rp|191-194}}  Most of this early work focused on the right eigenvalue problem. In the 1980s, R. M. W. Wood proved the existence of left eigenvalues.<ref name = Wood>{{Cite journal |last=Wood |first=R. M. W. |date=1985 |title=Quaternionic Eigenvalues |journal=Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=137–138 |doi=10.1112/blms/17.2.137 }}</ref>{{rp|137}} Subsequent work by W. So, L. Huang and others developed computational methods, localization theorems and classifications of left eigenvalues for low-dimensional quaternionic matrices.<ref name = HuangSo /> 

In the early 2000s, the subject expanded into infinite-dimensional operator theory through the development of slice hyperholomorphic function theory. This led to the introduction of the S-spectrum and the quaternionic functional calculus by F. Colombo, I. Sabadini, providing a complete framework for the [[spectral theory]] of quaternionic [[linear operators]].<ref name="Colomboetall" /> Recent work has also explored applications of this theory to [[Fractional calculus#Time-space fractional diffusion equation models|fractional difussion processes]]. <ref name = "Colomboetall18"/>

== Applications ==
[[Quaternion|Quaternionic]] [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalue]] problems appear naturally in quaternionic [[quantum mechanics]], where observables and evolution operators are represented by quaternionic linear operators.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Birkhoff |first1=Garrett |last2=Von Neumann |first2=John |date=1936 |title=The Logic of Quantum Mechanics |journal=Annals of Mathematics |volume=37 |issue=4 |pages=823–843 |doi=10.2307/1968621 |jstor=1968621 }}</ref>{{rp|836}} Quaternionic matrices are also used in [[applied mathematics]] and engineering, for instance colour [[Digital image processing|image processing]] and [[signal processing]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Miron |first1=Sebastian |last2=Flamant |first2=Julien |last3=Bihan |first3=Nicolas Le |last4=Chainais |first4=Pierre |last5=Brie |first5=David |date=September 2023 |title=Quaternions in Signal and Image Processing: A comprehensive and objective overview |journal=IEEE Signal Processing Magazine |volume=40 |issue=6 |pages=26–40 |doi=10.1109/MSP.2023.3278071 |bibcode=2023ISPM...40f..26M |url=https://hal.science/hal-04199725 }}</ref>{{rp|28}}

== Background == 
=== Quaternions === 
[[File:Cayley_Q8_multiplication_graph.svg|thumb|upright=1.2| Multiplication rules of the imaginary units]]
The [[quaternion]]s, denoted by <math>\mathbb{H}</math>, are a four-dimensional [[associative algebra]] over the [[Real number|real numbers]]. Every quaternion can be written uniquely in the form

<math> q=a+bi+cj+dk, </math>

where <math>a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}</math> and the imaginary units satisfy

<math> i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1. </math>

Unlike the real and [[Complex number|complex numbers]], quaternion multiplication is not commutative. For example,

<math> ij=k,\qquad\text{whereas}\qquad ji=-k. </math>

Every nonzero quaternion has a multiplicative inverse. The quaternions therefore form a [[Division ring#Relation_to_fields_and_linear_algebra|division ring]] (also called skew field), but not a field. This makes quaternionic linear algebra distinct to [[Linear algebra|real and complex linear algebra]].

=== Quaternionic vector spaces ===
Since quaternions form a [[Division ring#Relation_to_fields_and_linear_algebra|noncommutative division ring]], scalar multiplication on a [[quaternionic vector space]] must be specified to act either on the left or on the right. A left quaternionic vector space (or left <math>\mathbb H</math>-module) is an [[abelian group]] equipped with a scalar multiplication

<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
V\times\mathbb H&\to V\\ 
  (v,q)&\mapsto qv
\end{aligned}
</math>

satisfying the [[Vector space#Definition and basic properties|vector space axioms]]. Similarly, a right quaternionic vector space (or right <math>\mathbb H</math>-module) is an abelian group equipped with a scalar multiplication

<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
V\times\mathbb H&\to V\\
  (v,q)&\mapsto vq
\end{aligned}
</math>

satisfying the same axioms. Accordingly, two notions of quaternionic linear map arise.<ref name = Colomboetall11>{{cite book |title=Noncommutative Functional Calculus |series=Progress in Mathematics |date=2011 |volume=289 |doi=10.1007/978-3-0348-0110-2 |isbn=978-3-0348-0109-6 }}</ref>{{rp|136}}  If V is a right quaternionic vector space, a map <math>T:V\to V</math> is right-linear if

# for every <math>v,w\in V</math>, <math> T(v+w)=T(v)+T(w),</math>
# for every <math>v\in V</math> and <math>q\in\mathbb H</math>, <math> T(vq)=T(v)q .</math>

Similarly, if V is a left quaternionic vector space, a map <math>T:V\to V</math> is left-linear if

# for every <math>v,w\in V</math>, <math> T(v+w)=T(v)+T(w),</math>
# for every <math>v\in V</math> and <math>q\in\mathbb H</math>, <math> T(qv)=qT(v) .</math>

Once a basis has been chosen, every right-linear map on an <math>n</math>-dimensional right quaternionic vector space is represented by an  <math>n \times n</math> matrix with quaternionic entries. In this case [[matrix multiplication]] is defined in the usual way and satisfies  <math>A(vq)=A(v)q</math>,  thus being a right linear map.

==Right eigenvalue problem==
For a matrix <math>A\in M_n(\mathbb{H})</math>, the right eigenvalue problem consists of finding a nonzero vector <math>v\in\mathbb{H}^n</math> and a quaternion <math>\lambda\in\mathbb{H}</math> such that

<math> Av=v\lambda. </math>

The quaternion <math> \lambda </math> for which the above equation holds is called a right eigenvalue of <math> A </math>. The set of right eigenvalues of <math> A </math> is called right spectrum of <math> A </math>, denoted by <math> \sigma_R(A) </math>.<ref name = HuangSo />{{rp|106}} If <math> v</math> is replaced by <math> vq </math> for some nonzero quaternion <math> q </math>, the corresponding eigenvalue becomes <math> q^{-1}\lambda q</math>, since

<math> A(vq)=(vq) (q^{-1}\lambda q). </math>

This is the first distinctive feature of the right eigenvalue problem: in contrast with the classical problem, where an  <math>n \times n</math> matrix admits at most <math>n</math> distinct [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalues]], some quaternionic matrices admit an infinite number of eigenvalues. Nevertheless, the eigenvalues can be organized in a finite number of equivalence classes, also referred to as eigenvalue class.<ref name=Zhang/>{{rp|25}} The eigenvalue class generated by <math> \lambda </math> is defined by

<math> [\lambda]= \{\mu\in\mathbb{H} : \mu = q^{-1}\lambda q,\quad q\in\mathbb{H}\setminus\{0\}\} </math>

Zhang showed that the number of eigenvalue classes is finite.<ref name=Zhang>{{cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Fuzhen |title=Quaternions and matrices of quaternions |journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications |date=January 1997 |volume=251 |pages=21–57 |doi=10.1016/0024-3795(95)00543-9 }}</ref>{{rp|39}} The precise statement is the following

{{Math theorem| name = Theorem<ref name = Zhang/>{{rp|39}} | Let <math>A</math> be an <math>n \times n</math> matrix with quaternionic entries. Then <math>A</math> has exactly <math> n </math> eigenvalues classes. }}

Note that, if one is restricted the classic eigenvalue problem over the complex numbers, the eigenvalue classes are simply the [[Singleton (mathematics)|singletons]] <math> [\lambda]= \{\lambda\} </math>. Therefore the above theorem is a direct generalization of classic result: a complex matrix of size <math> n </math> has <math> n </math> (complex) eigenvalues.

=== Computing the right spectrum ===

Lee characterizes an algorithm to compute the eigenvalues of a quaternionic matrix <ref name = Lee />{{rp|255}} :

# Decompose the quaternionic matrix <math> A</math> as <math>A_1+A_2 j </math> with <math>A_1, A_2\in M_n(\mathbb{C})</math>. Consider the companion matrix associated with <math> A </math> (also called complex adjoint matrix or adjoint of the matrix <math> A </math> ) defined by <math>\chi(A) = \begin{pmatrix}
		A_1 & A_2 \\
		-\overline{A_2} & \overline{A_1}
\end{pmatrix}.
</math>
# Compute the eigenvalues of the matrix <math>\chi(A)</math>, also called the standard eigenvalues of <math>A</math>. As a complex matrix, one can use classic techniques to compute its eigenvalues.
# Each conjugate pair of eigenvalues <math>\lambda, \overline{\lambda}</math> of <math>\chi(A)</math> generates the same eigenvalue class <math>[\lambda]</math> of the original matrix <math>A</math>.

=== Canonical forms ===

The classical canonical forms of complex matrices admit extensions to the quaternionic context. In particular, the [[Schur decomposition|Schur decomposition]] and the [[Jordan normal form|Jordan normal form]] generalize to quaternionic matrices by using right eigenvalues, more specifically the standard eigenvalues.<ref name = Zhang />

Lee proved that any quaternionic matrix <math>A \in M_n(\mathbb{H})</math> is unitarily similar to an upper triangular matrix whose diagonal entries correspond to the standard eigenvalues of the matrix <math>A</math>.<ref name = Lee >{{Cite journal |last=Lee |first=H. C. |date=1948 |title=Eigenvalues and Canonical Forms of Matrices with Quaternion Coefficients |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy. Section A: Mathematical and Physical Sciences |volume=52 |pages=253–260 |jstor=20488503 }}</ref>{{rp|255-256}} Brenner later gave an alternative treatment of this result.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brenner |first1=J. L. |title=Matrices of quaternions |journal=Pacific Journal of Mathematics |date=September 1951 |volume=1 |issue=3 |pages=329–335 |doi=10.2140/pjm.1951.1.329 }}</ref>{{rp|331}} The precise statement is as follows.

{{Math theorem | name = Theorem<ref name = Lee />{{rp|256}}  | Let <math>A \in M_n(\mathbb{H})</math>. Then there exists a unitary matrix{{efn| Unitary in the sense of quaternions.  The definition is the same as for complex matrices but one requires [[Quaternion#Conjugation, the norm, and reciprocal|quaternionic conjugation]].}} <math>V</math> with quaternionic coefficients such that <math>V^*AV</math> is upper triangular, whose diagonal elements are the standard eigenvalues of  <math>A</math>. }}

Wiegmann proved that every quaternionic matrix is similar to a matrix in Jordan canonical form. The Jordan blocks are determined by the standard eigenvalues and classify quaternionic matrices up to similarity.<ref name = Wiegmann >{{Cite journal |last=Wiegmann |first=N. A. |date=January 1955 |title=Some Theorems On Matrices With Real Quaternion Elements |journal=Canadian Journal of Mathematics |volume=7 |pages=191–201 |doi=10.4153/CJM-1955-024-x }}</ref>{{rp|191-194}} The precise statement is as follows.

{{Math theorem | name = Theorem<ref name = Wiegmann />{{rp|194}} |Let <math>A \in M_n(\mathbb{H})</math>. Then there exists an invertible matrix P with quaternionic coefficients such that <math>P^{-1}AP</math> has the Jordan canonical form, whose diagonal elements are the standard eigenvalues of  <math>A</math>. }}

==Left eigenvalue problem==

In contrast with the right eigenvalue problem, the theory of left eigenvalues is less developed and exhibits several phenomena with no classic analogue. Their systematic study began through the work of Wood,<ref name = Wood/> Huang and So,<ref name = HuangSo>{{cite journal |last1=Huang |first1=Liping |last2=So |first2=Wasin |title=On left eigenvalues of a quaternionic matrix |journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications |date=January 2001 |volume=323 |issue=1–3 |pages=105–116 |doi=10.1016/S0024-3795(00)00246-9 }}</ref> and others. For a matrix <math>A\in M_n(\mathbb{H})</math>, a quaternion <math>\lambda </math> is called left eigenvalue of <math>A </math>  if there exists a nonzero vector <math>v\in\mathbb{H}^n</math> such that

<math> Av=\lambda v. </math>

The set of left eigenvalues of <math>A </math> is called left spectrum of <math>A </math> and its denoted by <math>\sigma_L(A) </math>.<ref name = HuangSo />{{rp|106}} Huang and So showed, even a <math>2\times 2 </math> quaternionic matrix can have both finite and infinite number of left eigenvalues.<ref name = HuangSo />{{rp|110}} Namely, the following theorem is proved

{{Math theorem | name = Theorem<ref name = HuangSo />{{rp|110}}  |Let <math>A = \begin{pmatrix} a& b \\ c & d\end{pmatrix} \in M_2(\mathbb{H})</math>. Then  <math> \sigma_L(A)</math> is infinite if and only if <math> bc\neq 0 </math>, <math> b^{-1}(a-d)</math>, <math> b^{-1}c \in\mathbb{R}</math> and <math> \Delta = (b^{-1}(a-d))^2+4b^{-1}c<0 </math>. In this case

<math>\sigma_L(A) = \left\{\frac{a+d}{2} + \frac{b}{2}x: \overline{x} = -x, |x|^2 = |\Delta| \right\}. </math>}}

Left eigenvalues do not have similar properties to right eigenvalues. For instance, unlike right eigenvalues, left eigenvalues are not invariant under similarity transformations. If <math> B=P^{-1}AP </math>, the left spectra of <math> A </math> and <math> B </math> need not coincide. Indeed, if <math> Av=\lambda v </math>, then

<math> B(P^{-1} v) =  P^{-1}\lambda v .</math>

Since quaternionic scalars do not commute with the entries of <math> P^{-1} </math>, the identity <math> P^{-1}\lambda v = \lambda P^{-1} v  </math> does not generally hold. Consequently, <math> P^{-1} v </math> need not be a left eigenvector of <math> B </math> associated with the same eigenvalue. For this reason, left eigenvalues do not give rise to a Jordan canonical form analogous to that associated with right eigenvalues.

==Infinite dimensional case==

The theory of quaternionic matrices extends to bounded linear operators on infinite-dimensional quaternionic [[Hilbert space|Hilbert]] and [[Banach space|Banach spaces]].<ref name = Alpay24>{{cite book |title=Quaternionic Hilbert Spaces and Slice Hyperholomorphic Functions |series=Operator Theory: Advances and Applications |date=2024 |volume=304 |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-73430-4 |isbn=978-3-031-73429-8 }}{{pn|date=September 2026}}</ref><ref name = Colomboetall11 /> In this setting, however, the classical notion of eigenvalue is insufficient for developing a spectral theory analogous to that of complex operators. Namely, the noncommutativity of the quaternions prevents the direct extension of the [[Spectral theory#Resolvent operator|classical resolvent operator]] <math> (A-\lambda I)^{-1} </math> to this setting.<ref name = Colomboetall18>{{cite book |title=Spectral Theory on the S-Spectrum for Quaternionic Operators |series=Operator Theory: Advances and Applications |date=2018 |volume=270 |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-03074-2 |isbn=978-3-030-03073-5 }}</ref>{{rp|3}}

For this reason, the <math>S</math>-spectrum was introduced.<ref name= Colomboetall>{{cite journal |last1=Colombo |first1=Fabrizio |last2=Sabadini |first2=Irene |last3=Struppa |first3=Daniele C. |title=A new functional calculus for noncommuting operators |journal=Journal of Functional Analysis |date=April 2008 |volume=254 |issue=8 |pages=2255–2274 |doi=10.1016/j.jfa.2007.12.008 }}</ref>{{rp|2263}} For a bounded right-linear operator <math>T</math>, the <math>S</math>-spectrum is defined as

<math> \sigma_S(T)=\{ s\in\mathbb{H} : T^2-2\operatorname{Re}(s)\,T+|s|^2I  \text{ is not invertible } \}.</math>

The <math>S</math>-spectrum generalizes several properties of the spectrum of a complex operator while respecting the quaternionic structure. Later it was shown to agree with the right spectrum of a quaternionic operator acting on a quaternionic right Banach space.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Carvalho |first1=Luís |last2=Diogo |first2=Cristina |last3=Mendes |first3=Sérgio |last4=Soares |first4=Helena |date=2024-12-20 |title=On the Relation Between S-Spectrum and Right Spectrum |journal=Complex Analysis and Operator Theory |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=17 |doi=10.1007/s11785-024-01631-0 }}</ref>{{rp|17}}
